A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DyePack research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and relocated sections and renumbered displays can be reliably matched.

before.justification: v1 reports original contamination-detection experiments on five models across MMLU-Pro, Big-Bench-Hard, and Alpaca, alongside dataset-size ablations and mixed-data experiments.

after.justification: v4 retains those experiments and adds Qwen-2.5-32B results in Table 3 and a benchmark-ranking analysis in Appendix I.

M1.justification: The output-space partitioning, independently sampled backdoor targets, majority-based activation rule, and binomial-tail detection procedure remain unchanged. LoRA is introduced as an experimental training configuration for the additional model.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same MMLU-Pro subjects, Big-Bench-Hard categories, Alpaca generation task, and mixed-data scenario. The additional 32B model does not introduce different datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically compares DyePack against competing contamination detectors. Newly cited methods are discussed only; Qwen-2.5-32B is an additional model being tested, rather than a competing detection method.

E3.justification: Section 4.4 adds evaluation of Qwen-2.5-32B using LoRA. Appendix I introduces score-distortion and ranking comparisons across existing configurations. The original dataset selections, zero-shot prompting, single-epoch training, and 10% backdoor replacement settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix I substantially broadens the supplementary analysis to whether backdoor injection preserves evaluation quality, examining score distortion, 100 pairwise ranking comparisons, and a ranking-reversal threshold using existing accuracy results. Section 4.4 also adds a larger-model generalization check. The original dataset-size, backdoor-count, and mixed-data analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions use the same exact binomial-tail FPR calculation. Neither reports experimental seeds, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests for its experiments. The added theoretical expectation is not a new empirical uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Table 3 adds Qwen-2.5-32B results: with eight backdoors, the contaminated model activates all eight on every dataset, yielding FPR probabilities of 1e-8 on MMLU-Pro and Alpaca and 1.7e-7 on Big-Bench-Hard. Appendix I newly reports stable clean-model rankings and an approximately 28.1% ranking-flip threshold. All retained result-table values are unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix I adds a derivation of expected relative accuracy distortion, defining p as the backdoor-to-clean sample ratio and obtaining a factor p/(1+p). Its accompanying claim of distortion decreasing as 1/p contradicts that formula. The original theorem, proof, and FPR corollaries are unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contribution: proactive, query-only contamination detection using multiple stochastic-target backdoors with computable FPR guarantees. The headline benchmark claims and numerical rates remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v4 newly argues that larger models may learn backdoor shortcuts more readily and interprets the added analysis as showing limited score distortion and preserved rankings. It also recommends evaluator-run leaderboards reporting clean-only accuracy. The existing limitations concerning attack success and lack of retroactive protection remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v4 adds a project repository link on the title page and identifies LoRA as the training approach for Qwen-2.5-32B. The original hardware and hyperparameter table is unchanged after renumbering; it does not provide configuration details for the new 32B experiment.

R1.justification: Beyond moving the earlier detailed comparison into Section 5, v4 adds discussion of VarBench, AntiLeakBench, LiveBench, and PaCoST, plus references supporting model-scale arguments and evaluator-run leaderboards. These extend the context while retaining the same central positioning relative to contamination detection and dataset ownership verification.

P1.justification: v4 integrates the former Appendix I comparison into Related Work, swaps the ordering of Appendices E and F, and adds Section 4.4 and a new Appendix I. It also clarifies stochastic targets in the introduction. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: v4 adds Table 3 for the 32B model, renumbers the original appendix tables as Tables 4–6, and relocates existing displays, including Figure 2. Figures 1–10 retain their content; the two-column presentation is preserved with localized layout and emphasis changes.

improvement.justification: The 32B LoRA experiment and ranking-stability analysis provide useful validation absent from v1; the reported 28.1% threshold is supported by Table 5. The project link and broader related-work discussion also improve usability and context. These gains are limited by missing 32B training details and the new appendix's incorrect 1/p scaling statement, while the established method and results remain intact.
